# Normal-dependent endpoint allocation: exact coupled erosion and menu dual

This is an exact optimization within a specified compatible erosion
family for three consecutive fibers. It allows the endpoint paying for
a tight contact to depend on the continuous normal. The resulting dual
retains the original finite cap menu, its supporting statuses, and the
original total mass. It does not assert that the dual is always positive
or optimize over every compatible body deformation.

## 1. The actual family of normal-dependent couplings

Let A,B,K be arbitrary positive convex bodies in R^d with
(A+B)/2 subset K. Choose y in int K, not necessarily in (A+B)/2. Use
the projective normalizer a of K-y and its positive convex decreasing
extension f from the ordinary projective-boundary theorem. Set

    H(n)=h_(K-y)(n)>0,
    b_* in argmin_B a.b, a_* in argmin_A a.x,
    U_A(n,x)=2H(n) f(1+a.((x+b_*)/2-y)),
    U_B(n,x')=2H(n) f(1+a.((a_*+x')/2-y)).                   (1)

Let t:S^(d-1)->[0,1] be continuous. Define the actual input erosions by

    A_e(t)={x:n.x+e t(n)U_A(n,x)<=h_A(n) for every n},
    B_e(t)={x:n.x+e(1-t(n))U_B(n,x)<=h_B(n) for every n},
    K_e={x:g_(K-y)(x-y)+e f(1+a.(x-y))<=1}.                 (2)

The fields in (2) are continuous and nonnegative, and convex in the
physical point for each fixed normal. Small positive e therefore gives
positive nested convex bodies. At every normal, monotonicity of f gives,
for x in A_e and x' in B_e and m=(x+x')/2,

    U_A(n,x), U_B(n,x') >= 2H(n) f(1+a.(m-y)).

Averaging the two input inequalities yields the defining inequality of
K_e. Thus

    (A_e(t)+B_e(t))/2 subset K_e                            (3)

EXACTLY for all sufficiently small e. The selected input depends on n;
it is not required to be the same endpoint at all contacts. No affine
center field or interior-midpoint assumption is needed.

The continuum-normal first-variation proof in
`candidate c56743c8d6824a18`,
Section 3, applies also when the speed vanishes at some normals. Its proof
uses only nonnegativity, a uniform upper bound, and continuity. In
particular (1-Ce)L subset L_e subset L still holds, and radial dominated
convergence gives the boundary integral of the prescribed speed. This
handles arbitrary nonsmooth bodies without a polyhedral approximation.

## 2. Signed normal measures retain the actual cap statuses

Fix a finite family of original ambient closed halfspaces H_j and a
normalization beta, with original mixed mass M. At fiber L=A or B,
write H_j^L for the ACTUAL restriction of the same ambient cap. Define
its boundary loss selector kappa_Lj by the following fixed statuses:

* If H_j^L cuts L properly, kappa_Lj(x)=1_(x in int H_j^L).
* If L subset H_j^L, including an inside supporting coincidence,
  kappa_Lj is one everywhere.
* If int L intersect H_j^L is empty, including an outside supporting
  coincidence, kappa_Lj is zero everywhere.

All fibers have positive d-volume. These cases cover the nonvertical
cuts, up to volume-null boundary choices, and also the whole/zero traces
of purely integer caps. In particular an outside supporting facet does
NOT acquire artificial loss from its closed boundary indicator.

Push forward the following finite signed measures by the almost-everywhere
outward normal map of the input boundary:

    sigma_Aj(E)=integral_(boundary A: n_A(x) in E)
                       (kappa_Aj(x)-beta)U_A(n_A(x),x)dS,
    sigma_Bj(E)=integral_(boundary B: n_B(x) in E)
                       (kappa_Bj(x)-beta)U_B(n_B(x),x)dS.    (4)

Let D_K be the source total loss and D_Kj its loss in H_j^K, with the
same status convention. Put r_Kj=D_Kj-beta D_K. Then the exact loss
surplus for the ORIGINAL cap and ORIGINAL total mass under (2) is

    r_j(t)=r_Kj+integral t d sigma_Aj+integral(1-t)d sigma_Bj
          =c_j+integral t d nu_j,
    c_j=r_Kj+sigma_Bj(S), nu_j=sigma_Aj-sigma_Bj.             (5)

All terms keep the original integer tilt; the endpoint caps have not
been independently optimized. The sign convention is that r_j>0 means
cap loss exceeds beta times total loss and hence gives a negative
normalized first response. For through-y middle caps,
D_Kj>=Gamma_d D_K, but that estimate is not substituted for the actual
D_Kj in the exact optimization below.

For a fixed finite critical cap cover with persistent slack covers at
other bases, positivity of every selected r_j is a sufficient actual
global descent certificate. The theorem below only characterizes this
specified fixed-row certificate. It does not assert that its failure
precludes reselecting caps, reequalizing a regular circuit, changing the
source, or using another compatible deformation.

## 3. Exact range, continuous realization, and the dual theorem

First allow arbitrary measurable 0<=t<=1 and set

    R={ (c_j+integral t d nu_j)_j : 0<=t<=1 }.                (6)

This is a compact convex subset of the finite-dimensional row space.
Convexity is immediate. For compactness choose a finite positive measure
mu dominating all |nu_j|, and write nu_j=g_j mu, |g_j|<=1. A sequence of
admissible t is bounded in L^2(mu); a weakly convergent subsequence exists.
Testing against indicators keeps its limit between zero and one, while
testing against the finitely many g_j preserves all row coordinates.
Thus R is closed and bounded. The case mu=0 is the singleton range.

Continuous t with 0<=t<=1 are dense for all the integrals in (5).
Indeed finite Radon measures on the compact sphere admit continuous
L^1 approximations to bounded measurable functions: approximate by simple
functions, place compact subsets inside their measurable level sets and
open supersets around them with arbitrarily small measure difference,
and interpolate continuously between zero and one. Clamp the final
approximation to [0,1]. One may enlarge mu by the two positive endpoint
cost measures to approximate all cap losses and total costs as well.
This preserves atoms and does not require cap-boundary regularity beyond
the exact selectors already built into (4). For d=1 the sphere is a
two-point space and no approximation is needed.

Consequently, a STRICTLY positive row vector in R is realized, to within
any smaller positive margin, by an actual continuous normal allocation
in (2). We do not claim exact continuous attainment of every boundary
point of R.

For a probability vector lambda on the finite row set, write

    r_Klambda=sum_j lambda_j r_Kj,
    sigma_Alambda=sum_j lambda_j sigma_Aj,
    sigma_Blambda=sum_j lambda_j sigma_Bj.

**Exact strict-feasibility theorem.** The following are equivalent:

1. There is a continuous t:S->[0,1] with r_j(t)>0 for EVERY row j.
2. For every probability vector lambda,

       r_Klambda+sigma_Blambda(S)
          +(sigma_Alambda-sigma_Blambda)^+(S)>0.             (7)

Equivalently, the minimum of the left side of (7) over the probability
simplex is strictly positive.

Proof. For any finite signed measure nu,

    sup_(0<=t<=1) integral t d nu=nu^+(S).                   (8)

This follows by choosing the indicator of its positive Hahn set; every
other t is bounded above by that value. Thus the expression in (7) is
the support function of the compact convex range R in direction lambda.
If R meets the open positive orthant, all these support values are
positive with a common lower bound, and continuous approximation proves
statement 1. Conversely, if it does not meet that open orthant, finite
dimensional separation supplies a nonzero lambda>=0 with
sup_(r in R)lambda.r<=0. Normalize its coordinate sum to one. Equation
(8) contradicts (7). The separation sign follows because a separating
functional must be nonnegative on the whole positive orthant, whose
infimum for that functional is zero.

Finally the support function is continuous in lambda: its Lipschitz
constant is bounded by a sum of the finite total variations and |c_j|.
The probability simplex is compact, so positivity for every lambda
implies a strictly positive minimum. This supplies the uniform strict
margin needed for actual small-parameter descent; pointwise positivity
without this compactness step would not suffice.

This proves an exact convex range/separation theorem for ONE already
specified menu and ONE compatible coupling family. It is not a minimax
swap between circuit choices and supporting allocations. The fixed
supporting statuses in (4) describe the actual loss of nested erosions
against the original caps; no freely chosen inside/outside allocation
is substituted for them.

## 4. Finite-facet implementation and what the result does not pay

For polytopal inputs the measures in (4) are supported on their finitely
many facet normals. Then the range (6) is a zonotope: one variable
t_n in [0,1] at each distinct shared or unshared normal, and (5) is a
finite affine map of that cube. Every such finite assignment extends
continuously to the sphere, so there is no approximation issue. The
strict feasibility problem is an exact finite LP. Its coefficients are
the original facet cap integrals, including full/empty support cases.

The dual (7) identifies the precise obstruction inside this family:
one nonnegative mixture of actual cap rows can have nonpositive best
normal-wise loss surplus even though every own-source cap separately
receives its projective Gamma payment. It does not replace that mixture
by a volume-only bound, delete input costs, or assume a paying choice
exists at every bad minimum.

The exact three-fiber calibration in Section 8 of the companion source
already demonstrates that allocation matters. The original balanced
support-ratio coupling is affine-neutral at beta=800/1803; the new
normal-center coupling pays Gamma_2, and t=1 in (2) pays40/87>Gamma_2.
These are different actual paths on the SAME critical menu. The new
result characterizes the best strict fixed-menu payment available from
the normal-dependent one-input family, without claiming global closure.

## 5. Exact active-contact overlap cost and a bounded descent criterion

The forcing can be restricted to actual active contact normals. Let

    Delta(n)=h_K(n)-h_((A+B)/2)(n)>=0,
    Z={n:Delta(n)=0}.

For delta>0 choose a continuous cutoff chi_delta equal to one where
Delta<=delta and zero where Delta>=2delta, between zero and one elsewhere.
In (2), replace the input fields by

    chi_delta(n)t(n)U_A(n,x),
    chi_delta(n)(1-t(n))U_B(n,x').                            (9)

These still give EXACT compatible erosions for every fixed delta and
continuous t, for all sufficiently small e. Where Delta<=delta, the full
one-input allocation argument applies. At every other normal the midpoint
remains in the original M=(A+B)/2 and has support gap greater than delta.
The target term is bounded by e max_n H(n) max_(m in M)f(1+a.(m-y));
choose e small enough that this is below delta. This also covers the
entire transition region. No hypothesis y in M or body smoothness is used.

Define the positive actual input cost measures on the normal sphere by

    mu_A(E)=integral_(boundary A:n_A(x) in E) U_A(n_A(x),x)dS,
    mu_B(E)=integral_(boundary B:n_B(x) in E) U_B(n_B(x),x)dS.

Their measure-theoretic overlap is the positive measure

    omega=mu_A wedge mu_B,
    d omega=min(d mu_A/d mu,d mu_B/d mu)d mu,
    mu=mu_A+mu_B.                                           (10)

This definition is independent of the chosen dominating measure. The
cost of (9) is exactly

    C_delta(t)=integral chi_delta t d mu_A
                     +integral chi_delta(1-t)d mu_B.

For a measurable allocation its minimum is integral chi_delta d omega:
at each normal choose the less costly endpoint. Continuous allocations
have the same infimum by Section 3's finite-measure approximation. As
delta decreases to zero, chi_delta tends pointwise to 1_Z and is bounded
by one. Therefore

    inf_(delta>0, continuous 0<=t<=1) C_delta(t)=omega(Z).    (11)

For the lower bound in (11), every cutoff equals one on Z and every
allocation has cost density at least the overlap there. For the upper
bound first choose delta small by dominated convergence, THEN choose a
continuous t approximating the measurable minimum. Finally choose the
erosion parameter e small for that fixed delta and t. No interchange of
a singular cutoff limit with the shape derivative is needed.

This exact cost has a concrete sufficient payment consequence. Suppose
a fixed finite cap cover through the assigned middle source controls its
deepest base planes, the original row masses equal Q=beta M_total, and
all other bases have persistent slack covers. If

    (Gamma_d-beta)D_K > beta omega(Z),                       (12)

then an actual compatible erosion of the form (9) strictly lowers the
global normalized depth. Indeed (12) lets us choose delta,t so that
the forced input cost C satisfies (Gamma_d-beta)D_K>beta C. Every cover
row loses at least Gamma_d D_K from the source alone, while its endpoint
losses are nonnegative. The total first loss is D_K+C. Hence every row
has a common strictly positive normalized loss surplus. The source
estimate is uniform in through-source cap directions; for the fixed
finite cover, ordinary small-e control and the original slack complete
the actual descent. Fixed supporting full/empty input caps cause no
problem because the bodies are nested; no supporting allocation has
been chosen to manufacture this lower bound.

In particular, if beta<Gamma_d and the restrictions of the two input
surface-area normal measures to Z are mutually singular, then omega(Z)=0
and (12) holds. The weights U_A,U_B are positive and bounded above and
below on their compact boundary bundles, so their cost measures have
exactly the same null sets as the corresponding surface-area measures.
Global mutual singularity is a stronger sufficient assumption. It must
not be inferred for two arbitrary smooth bodies.

For polytopes, (11) is the sum, over SHARED active facet normals, of the
smaller of the two actual weighted facet costs. A normal exposing a facet
in only one input contributes zero overlap: assign its erosion to the
other input, whose exposed face is lower dimensional and has zero first
volume cost. This recovers the geometric content of the archived
`candidate 860152d497c5cff4`. The present added interface
is an explicit finite-time compatible erosion for arbitrary convex bodies
and the exact weighted overlap formula (11), not a new claim that contact
stress or multiplier elimination itself was absent from the archive.

Condition (12) deliberately discards only nonnegative ENDPOINT CAP CREDIT;
it retains every forced endpoint volume cost. The exact row dual (7),
or its contact-band version with measures multiplied by chi_delta, can
be stronger. Nothing here asserts that the active overlap is small at
every attained bad minimum, that its contact cells are disjoint, or that
it is bounded by an occupied-parity count.

The difference is already exact on the genuine triangle calibration.
There Z is the whole normal sphere, D_K=9, and the cheaper input is A,
with omega(Z)=D_A^o=171/10. The left side of (12) is only 4/601, while
its right side is4560/601: the cost-only sufficient test fails decisively.
But each actual critical row loses8 in that same input, giving endpoint
loss surplus248/601. Added to the source surplus4/601, this is the
strictly positive total252/601 from the exact row test. Thus the proved
normal-allocation mechanism is genuinely stronger than its scalar
overlap-cost corollary; retaining SAME-cap endpoint credits matters even
in this simple compatible all-proper example.
